parsed.explanation: The parent regime imposes universal-exposure exposures: passport/visa marker policies that have stranded travellers, a fraud-lever visa cable targeting suspected trans applicants, facility bans across many states, documented custody abuses, and official 'gender ideology' threat-framing — placing the parent around the 0.40–0.45 band (cf. 0.45-A). This division adds a documented hostile layer: it sits in the 'worst laws passed' tier, defines sex by birth in statute, bans identity-facility use in schools, voids licence-marker changes (2026), allows amended birth certificates that retain the original marker, excludes gender identity from its hate-crime statute, and has a religious-liberties statute enabling service refusals. Per rule 12, a territory adding hostile layers cannot sit at its parent's average, so the score falls below the parent. Mitigations: the division's harshest rules are largely resident/school-facing rather than visitor-facing; national hate-crime recourse demonstrably worked (49-year sentence for a bias murder); local opinion (67–68%) favours non-discrimination protections, suggesting tier-3 friction rather than pervasive hostility. The mix — parent universal exposures plus an added sub-national hostile layer without local remedy, partially offset by national recourse and relatively supportive public opinion — resolves in the High Risk band at 0.34.
